name: bluewater-10-january
lines: It's the second week of January. Your phone hasn't rung since Tuesday.
And the worst part? You knew this was coming. It did the exact same thing last year.
So why does it feel like a surprise every single time?
Give me five minutes. Because the slow season isn't a marketing problem. It's a calendar problem. And you can fix a calendar.
Meet Rosa. She doesn't exist. Her January does.
Rosa runs a pressure washing company. Nine years. Two trucks. Three people who count on her for a paycheque.
From April to September, she can't keep up. Driveways. Decks. Siding.
In July she's booked three weeks out, and she's turning people away.
Then October comes. Then the rain. Then nothing.
December, she's at the kitchen table at midnight, moving money around to make payroll.
January, she cuts her prices in half. Half off everything. Just to make the phone ring.
A few people call. She works for almost nothing. And she teaches every one of them to wait for the sale.
February, she lets one of her crew go. A good one. By spring he's working for somebody else.
Here's what that costs. Say her busy months bring in thirty thousand, and her slow months bring in six.
Four slow months. That's a ninety six thousand dollar gap between her winter and her summer.
She'll never get all of it back. Winter is winter. But right now she isn't getting any of it.
One night she pulls out last year's calendar. And the year before that.
Same shape. Every year. A mountain in the middle, and a hole at each end.
It was never bad luck. It was a schedule. And nobody was running it.
Here's what's really going on. When you're busy, you stop marketing. You don't have time, and you don't need it.
But the work you're doing in July was won back in May. And the work you don't have in January, you never lined up in the fall.
Your slow season gets decided in your busy season.
So here are three moves. And you make every one of them while you're still busy.
Move one. Draw your year.
Take last year's invoices and add them up by month. Twelve numbers. That's all.
It takes about twenty minutes. And I'd bet you've never done it.
Now you can see the hole coming. Rosa circles October. That's where hers starts.
Then she counts back sixty days. August. That's when she has to start filling it.
Put it in your phone like a dentist appointment. August first. Start filling January.
Move two. Sell the slow month while you're standing in the driveway.
In July, Rosa finishes a driveway. The customer is thrilled. That's the best moment she'll ever have with them.
The old Rosa says thanks, and drives away.
The new Rosa says this. Your gutters will be full by November. Want me to put you down for the first week?
I'll book it now and text you the day before. No discount. No pressure. Just a date.
Say she finishes eight jobs a week, and one in four says yes. That's two bookings a week.
By the end of September, that's about forty jobs sitting in November. Before the slow season even starts.
Move three. Find the work that fits the weather.
Every trade has something people need in the off season. They just don't think to call you for it.
Rosa's is gutters in the fall, and holiday lights in December. Same ladders. Same crew. Same customers.
A heating company's might be tune ups before the cold. A landscaper's might be cleanups and snow.
Ask yourself one question. What do my customers need in my worst month, that my crew already knows how to do?
Then tell the people who already trust you. Not strangers. Your own list.
One short message in September. We're booking gutter cleaning for November. Want a spot?
Now, the shortcut. The half off sale.
It feels like action. But a panic discount in January cuts your pay in the month you can least afford it.
And it trains your customers to wait. Next year they'll ask you, when's the sale?
If you want to reward somebody, reward the early ones. Book by October, and your spot is saved. That's a reason, not a rescue.
One year later. The second week of January.
Rain on the window. Same kitchen table. Same calendar on the wall.
But this one has writing on it. Gutters. Lights coming down. Two storefronts that booked in the fall.
It isn't July. It was never going to be July.
But her phone buzzes. A reminder. Crew of three, eight o'clock, four jobs today.
And all three of her people are still on the payroll.
I can't promise you a full January. Nobody can. Slow seasons are real.
But there's a big difference between slow and empty.
Rosa didn't find new customers. She didn't spend a dollar on ads.
She used the months when the phone was ringing to fill the months when it wasn't.
Now, two traps to watch for.
Don't wait for the phone to go quiet before you act. By then it's too late for this year.
And don't invent a service your crew can't do well. One bad job in the off season can cost you a summer customer.
So do this tonight. Twelve numbers. Last year, by month.
Circle your worst one. Count back sixty days. Put that date in your phone.
Then write one sentence you can say at the end of every job between now and then.
Rosa's gap was ninety six thousand dollars wide. Yours has a number too. Go find it.
Draw the year. Book it while you're there. Find your winter work.
And if you want someone to map your year out with you, that's a conversation we're always up for at Bluewater.
